title: Ferromagnetic fluctuations and odd-parity pairing
summary: Separate triplet-pairing models from magnetic evidence, compare uranium compounds under stated conditions, and trace the limits of Knight shifts and critical fields.

review.scope: Selected primary abstracts, Sr2RuO4/Ran manuscript passages,2021 neutron extended-data text and2026 UTe2 publisher passages; independent spin, parity and angular-projection checks.
limitations: Full scientific acceptance, raw-data review and a comprehensive current literature survey remain open.
Author-manuscript checks do not establish final-version equivalence; several historical references are abstract-scoped.
Independent illustrations do not predict a material transition or establish a pairing kernel.
UTe2 4 K is a normal-state measurement temperature, not a superconducting transition. Different field/probe windows cannot be conflated.

claims.statement: Ferromagnetic fluctuations describe enhanced magnetic response near zero momentum transfer. They can support odd-parity pairing in specified models, but neither a large uniform susceptibility nor a large upper critical field identifies a superconducting spin state. Magnetic order, correlations, gap symmetry and the pairing interaction are separate questions. Fay and Appel calculated equal-spin p-state pairing from longitudinal fluctuations in an itinerant-electron model; this is a theoretical possibility, not a universal material classification.
claims.conditions: Effective ferromagnetic two-spin exchange; even-frequency single-orbital pairing; circular 2D Fermi surface a>b>0. Fay–Appel statements separately abstract-scoped.
claims.verificationScope: Independent spin/parity/quadrature checks; not reproduction of a material calculation or measured transition.

claims.statement: For a simple effective exchange $V=-J\boldsymbol{\sigma}_1\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}_2$ with $J>0$, the spin operator has eigenvalues $-3$ in the singlet and $+1$ in the triplet sector. The corresponding interaction eigenvalues are $+3J$ and $-J$. This independent two-spin illustration assumes a ferromagnetic effective interaction; it does not derive a material's exchange constant or its frequency dependence.

claims.statement: For even-frequency, single-orbital pairing, Fermi antisymmetry requires $\Delta(\mathbf k)=-\Delta^T(-\mathbf k)$. Writing a triplet matrix as $\Delta=(\mathbf d\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)i\sigma_y$ gives a symmetric spin matrix, so $\mathbf d(-\mathbf k)=-\mathbf d(\mathbf k)$. Odd parity here follows from these assumptions. Strong spin–orbit coupling requires a suitable pseudospin description; additional orbital or frequency structure changes this elementary argument.

claims.statement: The odd-parity projection $[V(\theta)-V(\theta+\pi)]/2$ retains odd angular harmonics. Since $0<r<1$, the strongest attractive odd harmonic in this example is $\ell=1$. Numerical quadrature checks the coefficients and projection. Crystal anisotropy, competing interactions and self-energy are absent: this example neither selects a universal p-wave state nor predicts a transition temperature.

claims.statement: UGe2 superconductivity was reported in a restricted pressure range within an itinerant-ferromagnetic setting. URhGe supplied ambient-pressure thermodynamic evidence for coexistence; UCoGe supplied ambient-pressure superconducting and ferromagnetic signatures. These primary abstracts support the historical observations, while microscopic volume overlap and a particular gap representation require more than proximity in a phase diagram. Corrected original links replace two inherited citation errors.

claims.statement: Lévy and colleagues reported a second superconducting pocket in URhGe around spin-axis reorientation near 12 T for field parallel to the crystal b axis, after low-field superconductivity had already disappeared. This is an orientation-specific re-entrant phenomenon. The original abstract suggests a connection to spin rotation; it does not uniquely establish a microscopic pairing kernel.

claims.statement: Pustogow and colleagues' 2019 Sr2RuO4 author manuscript reports a reduced oxygen-17 Knight shift and strong pulse-energy sensitivity. Its unstrained example uses an in-plane b-axis field of 0.7107 T; 20 mK is the base temperature, not a transition temperature. Selected methods explain why RF heating and different electronic/nuclear relaxation times can make a relaxation check insufficient. These observations challenge older unchanged-susceptibility interpretations; this entry does not infer a unique order parameter from them.

claims.statement: UTe2's discovery paper reported unusual anisotropic critical fields in a paramagnetic normal state. Its page 2 distinguishes a highest measured field of 20 T from an estimated zero-temperature b-axis value of 40 T. The estimate is not a measured endpoint. Historical triplet and ferromagnetic-pairing interpretations remain interpretations; the paper's schematic does not establish one continuous phase diagram shared by different uranium compounds.

claims.statement: Record field direction, pressure, composition, purity and temperature for each probe. Separate orbital/background contributions and pulse heating in Knight shifts; retain coupling, g-factor, multiband and orbital-limiting assumptions in critical-field comparisons. Combine symmetry-sensitive measurements with magnetic and superconducting volume evidence from the same sample. A bulk signal alone does not identify the mediating fluctuation.

claims.statement: In UTe2, Duan and colleagues reported a neutron resonance associated with antiferromagnetic wavevectors. Their extended-data comparison found no ferromagnetic signal above background in the stated measurement window. This is not absence of every possible small-momentum fluctuation at every field, energy and temperature; a resonance coupled to superconductivity also does not alone prove the direction of causation.

claims.statement: A study published on 29 April 2026 measured UTe2 magnetotropic response in pulsed fields up to 60 T at 4 K, where the studied superconducting phases were suppressed. It inferred enhanced transverse, near-zero-momentum susceptibility at high fields. Here transverse means perpendicular to the applied field, not an off-diagonal tensor component. These normal-state measurements differ from zero/low-field neutron conditions. The displayed 300 mK superconducting boundaries came from earlier work, and 4 K must not be recorded as this experiment's superconducting transition.

claims.statement: Fluctuations can enhance attraction while also renormalizing quasiparticles and affecting pair breaking. Fay–Appel's model gives a maximum followed by a decrease of calculated transition temperature toward the magnetic transition. Neither that model nor the elementary angular projection proves a universal optimum at a ferromagnetic quantum critical point. Longitudinal/transverse spectral weight, spin–orbit coupling and band structure must be specified.

claims.statement: Treat small-momentum magnetic response as a candidate-screening observation. Test whether a proposed kernel simultaneously explains symmetry constraints, normal-state responses and field/pressure trends under matched conditions. Keep negative observations and alternative channels. The recent UTe2 comparison illustrates why distinct experiments should retain their conditions instead of being reduced to a single ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic label. Selected source passages and model checks here leave full scientific acceptance open.
